text: Soon afterward Jesus traveled through the towns and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with him,
and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and diseases: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;

versions.text: and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and diseases: Mary, called Magdalene, out of whom seven demons had gone;
versions.explanation: "out of whom seven demons had gone" is slightly stilted for oral reading; "from whom seven demons had gone out" flows more naturally and matches the verb ἐξεληλύθει (gone out).

text: Joanna, the wife of Herod's steward Chuza; Susanna; and many others, who provided for them out of their own means.
When a large crowd had gathered, with people streaming in to him from town after town, he spoke this parable:
"A farmer went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the path, where it was trampled underfoot and the birds of the sky ate it up.
Some fell on rock, and when it came up it withered, because it had no moisture.
Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it.
And some fell into good soil, and it grew and produced a hundredfold." As he said this, he called out, "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear!"
His disciples asked him what this parable meant.
He said, "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest I speak in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

versions.text: He said, "To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to the rest they come in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.
versions.explanation: The pronoun "they" has no clear antecedent when heard aloud (the mysteries? the parables?). Supplying the implied verb from Jesus' own speech clarifies the elliptical Greek without adding content.

text: This is what the parable means: The seed is the word of God.
The ones along the path are those who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word away from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
The ones on the rock are those who receive the word with joy when they hear it, but they have no root; they believe for a while, and in the time of testing they fall away.
As for what fell among the thorns, these are the ones who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the worries, riches, and pleasures of life, and their fruit never ripens.
But the seed in the good soil—these are the ones who hear the word with a noble and good heart, hold it fast, and bear fruit with patient endurance.
"No one lights a lamp and then covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, he sets it on a stand, so that those who come in can see the light.
For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and nothing concealed that will not be made known and brought to light.
So pay attention to how you listen. For to the one who has, more will be given; and from the one who does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away."
Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd.
He was told, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wanting to see you."
He answered them, "My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it."
One day he got into a boat with his disciples and said to them, "Let us cross over to the other side of the lake." So they set out.
As they sailed, he fell asleep. A violent squall came down on the lake, and the boat was filling up, and they were in danger.
They went to him and woke him, saying, "Master, Master, we are perishing!" He got up and rebuked the wind and the raging waves; they subsided, and there was a calm.
Then he said to them, "Where is your faith?" Filled with fear and amazement, they said to one another, "Who then is this, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?"

versions.text: Then he said to them, "Where is your faith?" Filled with fear and amazement, they said to one another, "Who then is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him."
versions.explanation: The Greek is a single question introduced by ὅτι; splitting it into a question plus a flat statement loses the tone of astonished wonder and the causal link.

text: They sailed on to the region of the Gerasenes, which lies across the lake from Galilee.
As he stepped ashore, a man from the town who was possessed by demons met him. For a long time he had worn no clothes and had not lived in a house, but among the tombs.

versions.text: As he stepped ashore, a man from the town met him who was possessed by demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes and had not lived in a house, but among the tombs.
versions.explanation: The relative clause "who was possessed by demons" is separated from its antecedent "a man," making it sound as though it modifies "him" (Jesus). Placing the clause next to "man" removes the ambiguity.

text: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him, shouting at the top of his voice, "What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me!"

For Jesus had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Many times it had seized him; he was kept under guard, bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the wilderness.
Jesus asked him, "What is your name?" "Legion," he said, for many demons had entered him.
And they begged him not to order them to go into the abyss.
A large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and the demons begged Jesus to let them enter the pigs. He gave them permission.
So the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
When those tending the pigs saw what had happened, they ran off and reported it in the town and in the countryside.
People went out to see what had happened, and when they came to Jesus, they found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind—and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed.
Then the whole crowd from the region of the Gerasenes asked Jesus to leave them, for they were gripped with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
The man from whom the demons had gone out begged to go with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying,
"Return home and tell how much God has done for you." So he went and proclaimed throughout the whole town how much Jesus had done for him.
When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they had all been waiting for him.
Then a man named Jairus came—he was a ruler of the synagogue. He fell at Jesus' feet and pleaded with him to come to his house,
because his only daughter, about twelve years old, was dying. As Jesus went, the crowds pressed in around him.
And a woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years. She had spent all she had on physicians, yet no one could heal her.
She came up behind him and touched the edge of his cloak, and immediately her bleeding stopped.
"Who touched me?" Jesus asked. When they all denied it, Peter said, "Master, the crowds are surrounding you and pressing in on you."
But Jesus said, "Someone touched me, for I perceived that power had gone out from me."

versions.text: But Jesus said, "Someone touched me; I know that power has gone out from me."
versions.explanation: The Greek ἔγνων is aorist ('I perceived/knew'), describing what Jesus sensed at that moment, not a present state ('I know'). The causal γάρ ('for') is also dropped in the current rendering, losing the logical link between the two clauses.

text: Seeing that she could not remain hidden, the woman came trembling and fell down before him. In the presence of all the people she told why she had touched him and how she had been healed at once.
He said to her, "Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace." [Footnote: Or 'your faith has made you well'; the Greek verb means both to save and to heal.]

versions.text: He said to her, "Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace."
versions.explanation: The verb σέσωκέν carries both 'saved' and 'healed' senses; in this healing context a brief footnote would help hearers understand the double meaning without changing the main text.

text: While he was still speaking, someone came from the synagogue ruler's house and said, "Your daughter is dead. Do not trouble the teacher any longer."

versions.text: While he was still speaking, someone came from the house of the synagogue ruler and said, "Your daughter is dead. Do not trouble the teacher any longer."
versions.explanation: The Greek reads simply 'from the synagogue ruler'; 'the house of' is a supplied clarification. The possessive form is shorter and reads more smoothly aloud while conveying the same sense.

text: But Jesus heard it and said to him, "Do not be afraid. Only believe, and she will be saved."
When he came to the house, he let no one go in with him except Peter, John, and James, and the child's father and mother.
Everyone was weeping and mourning for her, but he said, "Do not weep; she is not dead but sleeping."
And they laughed at him, because they knew she was dead.
But he took her by the hand and called out, "Child, get up!"
Her spirit returned, and she stood up at once. Then he directed that she be given something to eat.
Her parents were astounded, but he ordered them to tell no one what had happened.
